Mongolia: accused of taking a $25 million bribe, President Khurelsukh announces his resignation

On Tuesday 17 November, Mongolian President Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh announced he was stepping down, three days after being accused of receiving $25 million linked to a mining railway project. He denies everything and says he is leaving so the investigation can proceed. Parliament still has to accept his resignation.
Ukhnaagiin Khurelsukh made the announcement at a press conference at the State Palace in Ulaanbaatar, accepting the investigation demanded by the Democratic Party, the main opposition force [5][2].
He says he was "falsely accused of serious crimes" and is leaving so that investigations can establish the truth and his honour can be restored [2][4].
The accusation comes from Nyambaatar Khishgee, a former mayor of Ulaanbaatar who belongs to a rival faction of the Mongolian People's Party, the ruling party the president comes from [1].

On Saturday 14 November, the former mayor claimed that Khurelsukh had received $25 million in connection with the Tavantolgoi-Gashuunsukhait railway, which carries coal from the Tavan Tolgoi deposits [3][1].

The contract was awarded in 2019, when Khurelsukh was prime minister, to the Bodi International conglomerate, without a tender according to the accusation; the group denies paying any bribe to officials [3][1].

On Monday 16 November, all 42 MPs of the Democratic caucus backed setting up a parliamentary inquiry committee and demanded the publication of the coal sales contracts of state miner Erdenes Tavan Tolgoi [3].
Two other officials named, the deputy minister of justice and home affairs and the head of the cabinet secretariat, also announced their resignation, according to AP [1].
Key takeaway: the head of state of a country that matters for raw materials is falling over a corruption case tied to coal, the heart of Mongolia's economy [3][1].

The resignation is not yet effective: under the law on the presidency, the State Great Khural, the 126-member parliament, decides whether to accept it; until then, Khurelsukh stays in office [6]. Parliament was due to meet this week to vote, according to AP [1].
If it is accepted, the speaker of parliament, Sandag Byambatsogt, will serve as interim president, and a presidential election must be held within four months, according to AFP [2].

The affair comes on top of months of political turmoil, infighting within the ruling party and youth protests against corruption and inequality [2]. An expert quoted by AP also sees a political manoeuvre that could let Khurelsukh run for another office later and polish his image [1].

For you, the direct effect is small: Mongolia carries little weight in France's trade. But it is a good example of how mining contracts (coal, copper) attract corruption in resource-rich countries, and how an investigation can bring down a head of state [3][2]. Watch the parliamentary vote this week and the date of the early presidential election [1][2].
